Isserles' glosses on the Shulchan Aruch

category: halakhic glosses (Ashkenazi glosses on a code of law)

date.note: Composed by Moses Isserles of Krakow (the Rema, c. 1530-1572) and printed interwoven with Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch from the Krakow editions onward (from c. 1569-1571). The glosses follow the fourfold structure of the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, Choshen Mishpat), inserted siman by siman and marked in the text as a Hagah ('gloss'). The openly-auditable Hebrew on Sefaria for Orach Chayim is the Maginei Eretz edition (Lemberg, 1893).

summary: The Mappah ('The Tablecloth') is the set of glosses composed by Moses Isserles of Krakow (the Rema) and printed alongside, interwoven with, Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch, recording Ashkenazi practice (minhag Ashkenaz) where it diverges from Karo's largely Sephardic rulings. So that Karo's 'Set Table' (the Shulchan Aruch) and Isserles' 'Tablecloth' (the Mappah) together form the standard code of Jewish law for both Sephardim and Ashkenazim.
description:
The Mappah ('The Tablecloth') is the collective title of the glosses (Hebrew hagahot) that Moses Isserles of Krakow (the Rema, c. 1530-1572) composed on Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch. The name is a deliberate pairing with Karo's title: Karo called his code the Shulchan Aruch, 'the Set Table', and Isserles called his layer of glosses the Mappah, 'the Tablecloth' spread over that Set Table. This entry presents the work's function and its standing as attributed features of the text and its reception in the tradition, not as claims the editor affirms.

Karo's Shulchan Aruch had stated the practical law in brief, following as a general rule the majority among three earlier authorities Karo took as pillars (Isaac Alfasi, Maimonides, and Asher ben Yehiel), a procedure reflecting the largely Sephardic and Mediterranean tradition in which he worked. Its rulings did not always match the customs of Ashkenazi communities. Isserles' glosses supply, siman by siman, the ruling customary among Ashkenazim and the position of the later authorities (the Acharonim) where it differed, so that an Ashkenazi reader could use the same code. The glosses are printed interwoven with Karo's text and marked as a Hagah ('gloss'), the base text carrying Karo's ruling and the gloss the Ashkenazi one, and they follow the fourfold structure of the Shulchan Aruch through all four parts (Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, Choshen Mishpat).

The interweaving is visible from the very first ruling of the code. To Karo's opening charge at Orach Chayim 1:1, that one should 'strengthen himself like a lion to get up in the morning to serve his creator', the Mappah's opening gloss adds the verse 'I have set the Lord always before me' (shiviti, Psalm 16:8), calling it 'a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God', and it develops the theme of the constant awareness of God with reference to Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed (III:52). This opening gloss, read line-by-line on the open text of Sefaria, is the openly-auditable primary that carries the Mappah's authorship (by Isserles) and its function (an Ashkenazi layer over Karo's base) in the text itself.

Because the Mappah and the Shulchan Aruch were printed together, Karo's rulings interleaved with Isserles' glosses, the combined work spoke to both major branches of practice at once, and it came in the reception of the tradition to be treated as the central and authoritative code of halakha across both Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities, drawing a vast later literature of commentary and super-commentary around it. This entry describes that standing as the position the combined work holds within the tradition and in its reception; it does not itself rule the code binding, and it attributes the code's authority to how it has been received. The difference between the two rulings, Sephardic in the base text and Ashkenazi in the gloss, is described here as a difference of received communal practice, not ranked or adjudicated by the editor.
